# UEFN + Verse Master Reference — v42.20

**Purpose:** Single-source technical reference for Google AI Studio / Gemini working on UEFN and Verse projects.

**Target UEFN release:** 42.20

**Reference date:** 2026-09-29

**Platform boundary:** UEFN / Fortnite ecosystem only.

**Critical limitation:** The three supplied generated digests were generated from Fortnite Release 42.00. They are preserved below as immutable API baselines. Epic's public Verse API Reference page is currently labeled version 42.10, while Epic's 42.20 release notes document additional changes. Therefore this document must NOT be treated as a complete replacement for a fresh project-generated 42.20 digest. When a fresh 42.20 project digest exists, it has higher authority than this document.

## Authority Hierarchy

1. Fresh project-generated Verse / asset digests from the actual project.
2. Actual project source code and generated interfaces.
3. This master reference.
4. Current official Epic UEFN / Fortnite documentation and release notes.
5. Carefully selected community material for issue investigation only.
6. Model memory.

## Hard Rules

- UEFN is not interchangeable with generic Unreal Engine.
- Do not import UE-only gameplay/API assumptions into UEFN.
- Blueprint Visual Scripting is not available for gameplay/custom scripts in UEFN.
- Verse is the gameplay scripting authority unless UEFN explicitly exposes another supported system.
- Generated digests are immutable reference material.
- Never invent APIs, namespaces, fields, events, classes, or asset-generated symbols.
- Version-sensitive facts must be tied to a version.
- Experimental APIs must remain marked experimental.
- Deprecated APIs must remain marked deprecated until the current project digest proves otherwise.
- Existing project architecture must be analyzed before new systems are created.
- Reuse before creation.
- Do not store redundant mutable state when it can be derived.
- Preserve intended behavior, not accidental implementation.

## UEFN vs Unreal Engine Boundary

UEFN shares technology with Unreal Engine, but it has meaningful capability differences. Epic explicitly documents that Blueprint objects can appear in UEFN workflows such as materials and animation, while Blueprint Visual Scripting is not available for gameplay or other custom scripting in UEFN.

**Implementation rule:** Do not solve a UEFN gameplay problem with a generic UE Blueprint tutorial or a UE-only API. Verify the capability in UEFN documentation and the project's actual API surface first.

Official:
- https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/uefn-vs-ue-in-unreal-editor-for-fortnite

# 1. Current Version State: 42.00 → 42.20

## 42.00 baseline

Relevant 42.00 changes included:

- Unreal MCP became available in UEFN, allowing compatible agentic tools to interact with the editor.
- Touch input gestures through Virtual Pointer exited Experimental status.
- An Experimental code-native Ability System became available in Verse.
- UEFN Physics was moved to Island Settings.
- UEFN UI feature examples were expanded around Verse UI, Scene Graph UI, device UI, UI art, and full-feature examples.
- Scene Graph remained a Beta system with known limitations/instability.

Official:
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/42-00-fortnite-ecosystem-updates-and-release-notes

## 42.10 changes relevant to this reference

- Social Synergy API became available in Verse for party membership detection.
- The Experimental Verse Camera API received Blend and Cut transitions.
- An editor validator change enforced that non-`<concrete>` types cannot be used where `concrete_subtype(foo)` requires a concrete type; existing code using invalid combinations needs adjustment.
- Mobile Preview received expanded device selection support.

Official:
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/42-10-fortnite-ecosystem-updates-and-release-notes

## 42.20 changes relevant to this reference

### Channel API

Verse gained methods for creators to create, remove, and manipulate custom voice/text communication channels. These can be used for teams, zones, spectators, or other communication groups.

### Marketplace namespace move

Marketplace and entitlement Verse APIs moved from:

```text
/Fortnite.com/Marketplace
```

to:

```text
/UnrealEngine.com/Marketplace
```

Existing Fortnite namespace symbols remain available as aliases, but new projects should use `/UnrealEngine.com/Marketplace` and older imports should be migrated when appropriate to remove deprecation warnings.

### In-World UMG fix

42.20 fixed an issue where only one instance of an In-World UMG widget could render its Verse-bound values when multiple instances of the same widget class were present.

### Editor / project changes

42.20 also added new warnings for invalid Experimental Inventory settings.

### Memory tooling

Epic states that future releases will remove the memory thermometer from running sessions as memory guidance moves into profiling tools with real-time reporting and asset-level breakdowns.

### Rocket Racing

On October 1, 2026, Rocket Racing leaves Fortnite; islands built with Rocket Racing templates are being unpublished and new/update publishing is disabled. Rocket Racing developer tools such as the Track Spline Tool, Boost Pads, Volume Hazards, and Spawner devices were migrated so racing projects can be built without the template.

Official:
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/42-20-fortnite-ecosystem-updates-and-release-notes

## Public Verse API version caveat

Epic's public Verse API Reference is currently labeled **42.10**. Use it as a verified official API reference, but do not infer that every 42.20 API change is represented there.

Official:
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/fortnite/verse-api

Use the layer that owns the behavior. Do not force world placement into UMG layout, do not rebuild widget UI in Verse UI unnecessarily, and do not create Verse state for values already owned by a native device when the device already exposes the required behavior.

# 3. Verse Language Hard Reference

## Mutation

Verse mutations use `set`.

```verse
set Value = NewValue
```

## Failure and effects

A function with `<decides>` can fail; calling it is a failable expression. A function definition with `<decides>` also requires `<transacts>` so the work inside can roll back on failure.

A function with no exclusive effect is no-rollback. Its actions cannot be rolled back.

Official references:
- https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/decides
- https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/transacts
- https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/effect

## Failure-context rule

Do not place an expression that cannot legally execute in a failure context inside that failure context.

Common repair pattern:

```verse
Result := SomeNoRollbackOrOtherwiseIncompatibleCall()
if (Result?):
    ...
```

This is not a universal requirement for every `decides` function. Check the actual effects.

## Effect hierarchy

Epic's current glossary documents the exclusive-effect hierarchy as:

```text
transacts
  ↓
varies
  ↓
computes
  ↓
converges
```

Higher exclusive effects include the properties of lower effects.

## Containers and common language constructs

Use the generated digest for exact signatures and availability of:

- arrays
- maps
- optionals
- tuples
- generators
- classes
- structs
- interfaces
- enums
- types / subtypes
- generic types
- castable types
- weak maps
- persistable classes

Do not infer exact signatures from memory when the digest can be inspected.

## Concurrency

Use Verse concurrency primitives exposed by the current digest. Key concepts include:

- `Sleep`
- `race`
- `rush`
- `branch`
- `sync`
- event waiting
- task lifetime
- cancellation

Prefer event-driven logic over polling where an event exists.

## Async lifetime

Every spawned coroutine or repeating loop should have a reason to exist and a way to stop or become irrelevant.

Avoid duplicate background loops monitoring the same state.

# 6. Island Settings / Mode Settings / Device Precedence

Do not design Verse logic in isolation from island and device configuration.

For sensitive behavior, identify the authority explicitly:

1. Island Settings baseline
2. Native device override
3. Mode / game configuration
4. Team / class configuration
5. Runtime Verse state

Do not assume Verse automatically overrides a native device or island rule.

Inspect, at minimum, when relevant:

- Max Players
- Join In Progress
- spawn behavior
- spawn immunity
- spawn limits
- after-last-spawn behavior
- post-game spawn location
- team assignment
- score behavior
- rounds
- Team Settings & Inventory overrides
- Class Designer overrides

Join In Progress behavior must be reconciled with engine/device settings rather than assumed to be superseded by Verse.

Scene Graph is a Verse-native world/entity system in UEFN. Epic currently documents Scene Graph as a Beta feature and recommends caution when shipping with it.

Official:
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/getting-started-in-scene-graph-in-fortnite
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/scene-graph-known-issues-in-fortnite

## Core concepts

- transform
- local vs global transform
- prefab
- Verse component
- enableable components
- runtime entities
- entity spawning / removal
- component lookup
- entity queries

## Device boundary

Scene Graph entities/components/prefabs are not directly interchangeable with standard Creative devices. Use Verse as the integration layer when connecting Scene Graph systems to device systems.

## Current known issue category

Scene Graph remains Beta and Epic documents limitations/known issues including asset availability constraints, prefab override limitations, and transform/negative-scale edge cases.

# 8. Prefabs

Prefabs are reusable entity/component compositions.

Use them for reusable world structures, entity compositions, and systems that benefit from instance-level overrides.

Project-created prefabs are exposed to Verse through the project's generated `Assets.digest.verse` representation.

Important concepts:

- prefab asset
- prefab instance
- child entities
- components
- overrides
- nested prefab structure
- transforms
- external/internal entity files where supported
- Verse exposure

Do not assume a prefab's internal entity hierarchy is recursively discovered by arbitrary API calls. Inspect the actual generated/project API.

Official:
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/getting-started-in-scene-graph-in-fortnite

# 9. UMG / UI

## UMG User Widget

UMG remains the design layer for UI layout and presentation.

Common widget types include:

- Canvas
- Overlay
- Stack Box
- Grid / Uniform Grid
- Size Box
- Scale Box
- Scroll Box
- Text Blocks
- Images
- Buttons
- Materials
- nested User Widgets
- animations

## Verse Fields

Verse Fields connect data in Verse to UMG properties/events through View Bindings.

Epic introduced Verse Fields in UMG in 38.00. The source report supplied with this project identifies supported field types including `logic`, `int`, `float`, `message`, `material`, and `texture`.

Official:
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/38-00-fortnite-ecosystem-updates-and-release-notes

## View Bindings

View Bindings are the UI wiring layer between Verse Fields and UMG properties/events.

Typical pattern:

```text
Verse state
  ↓
Verse Field
  ↓
View Binding
  ↓
UMG property/event
  ↓
Visible UI / Verse event handling
```

## Verse UI

Screen-space UI through `player_ui` and related Verse widget APIs is distinct from UMG User Widgets.

Do not substitute one for the other without a reason.

## In-World UMG

An in-world User Widget is still a UMG User Widget, but UEFN exposes a corresponding Scene Graph entity representation.

Example:

```text
UW_Scoreboard
UW_Scoreboard_entity
```

Use the User Widget/Verse Fields layer for visual/data design and the `_entity` layer for world-space placement, hierarchy, attachment, spawning, and entity behavior.

Epic specifically states that when modifying the world widget entity's behavior, access the entity class rather than only the widget class.

Official:
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/inworld-user-widgets-using-scene-graph-in-fortnite

## In-World UMG size

World-space size is not the same thing as ordinary UMG pixel layout size. Small widgets may need a larger Scene Graph transform scale to be visibly readable in the world.

## Multiple instances

42.20 fixed an issue where only one instance of an In-World UMG widget could display its Verse-bound values when multiple instances of the same widget class existed.

Large-scale UEFN projects should treat performance as architecture.

Inspect:

- unnecessary Verse loops
- repeated searches
- repeated conversions/formatting
- duplicated UI updates
- duplicate subscriptions
- tasks without termination
- needless device calls
- excessive Scene Graph queries
- unnecessary entity/component lookup
- redundant state synchronization
- over-instantiated devices/entities
- expensive materials/assets
- mesh complexity
- texture size
- draw calls
- LOD/streaming behavior
- profiling data

Epic's current UEFN tooling includes project-size/memory analysis and profiling tools. 42.20 notes that future releases will move memory guidance into profiling tools with real-time reporting and asset-level breakdowns.

# 27. Architecture Patterns for Large UEFN Projects

## Single Responsibility

Each system should have a clear owner and purpose.

## Reuse Before Creation

Search first; extend existing infrastructure whenever appropriate.

## One Source of Truth

One canonical mutable state value where possible.

## Derived State

Compute inverse/derived state instead of storing duplicate booleans.

## Event-Driven Design

Prefer events over polling.

## Explicit Ownership

Know which subsystem owns each mutable value.

## Thin Device Layer

Use native devices for native responsibilities and Verse for orchestration/custom behavior when that reduces complexity.

## Scene Graph Components

Use components where Scene Graph owns the object behavior. Do not automatically convert every device into a component or every system into an entity.

## UI / Gameplay Separation

Keep gameplay state independent from visual presentation. Feed UI through the intended UI layer/Verse Fields rather than duplicating gameplay state just for UI.

## Pure Verse Classes

Non-device classes can be useful for pure logic, but do not create classes purely to hide a single line of logic. Prefer clear ownership.

## Manager Discipline

A manager must have a real responsibility. Do not accumulate giant manager classes or create multiple managers for the same domain.

---

# 28. Codebase Refactoring Rules

A refactor may:

- remove dead code
- merge equivalent functions
- remove inverse state
- merge managers
- reduce event chains
- remove unused fields
- remove abandoned prototypes
- reduce task count
- replace polling with events
- consolidate ownership
- reuse Utility.verse
- simplify APIs
- move logic to a better owner

Do not preserve accidental complexity merely because it already exists.

### Redundancy examples

Bad:

```verse
var IsLocked : logic = false
var IsActive : logic = false
```

when the two values always represent the same state in opposite forms.

Better:

```text
Store one canonical state value.
Derive the inverse when needed.
```

Bad:

```text
Create CurrencyFormatter()
```

when `Utility.verse` already provides `FormatNumber`.

Bad:

```text
Create another message helper
```

when `StringToMessage` already covers the use case.

---

# 29. Code Delivery Rules

When changing an existing file, estimate meaningful code-line modification.

- `< 40%` materially modified → snippets only.
- `>= 40%` materially modified → full file.

The threshold is about actual implementation changes, not formatting or comment churn.

For multiple changed files, apply the rule independently.

Never return unchanged files.

---

# 30. Requirements Gate / Clarification Behavior

When the user describes a feature concept but important gameplay/product rules are unspecified:

1. Do not invent them.
2. Ask focused questions.
3. Group questions by system.
4. Avoid implementation until the answers determine architecture.

Example feature:

> "Add a shop to the game to sell player cosmetics."

Relevant questions may include:

- What cosmetic categories exist?
- What currency is spent?
- How is currency earned?
- Are prices fixed or tiered?
- Are items permanently owned?
- What happens when an already-owned item is selected?
- Does the shop rotate?
- Does it use the existing customization system?
- What persistence model should own the purchase state?

Do not ask questions whose answers do not affect implementation.

# Appendix A — Verbatim `DEVICE_AND_ISLAND_SETTINGS_REFERENCE(2).md`

# Device & Island Settings Reference

## Purpose

The shooter engine exists inside UEFN's platform rules. Do not design Verse in isolation from Island Settings and native devices.

Epic's current Island Settings documentation describes Island Settings as baseline gameplay configuration and explicitly notes that device settings such as Team Settings & Inventory and Class Designer can override relevant island settings.

Official references:

- Island Settings: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/island-settings-in-uefn-and-fortnite-creative
- UEFN Island Settings: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/island-settings-in-unreal-editor-for-fortnite
- Mode Settings: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/fortnite/mode-settings-in-fortnite-creative
- Event Browser: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/event-browser-in-fortnite-creative
- Verse API: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/uefn/verse-api
- In-World User Widgets: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/inworld-user-widgets-using-scene-graph-in-fortnite

## Useful native devices

### Button

Use for explicit physical interactions such as entering a queue, selecting a mode, starting a vote, or invoking admin/test functions.

### Switch

Use for persistent/visible physical toggles such as Auto Queue preferences.

### Trigger

Use as a generic event bridge when other devices/systems need to invoke or react to Verse logic.

### Timer

Use when native timing/countdown behavior is useful.

### Teleporter

Use for lobby/arena movement and as part of a spawn/teleport adapter.

### Mutator Zone

Useful for physical arena/objective areas and player enter/exit events.

### Player Counter

Useful when an area needs native presence/counting behavior.

### Tracker

Useful for player or objective tracking where its native behavior matches the engine need.

### Score Manager

Useful when native score behavior should be used rather than duplicating it.

### Team Settings & Inventory / Class systems

Useful for team/class configuration, inventory behavior, and native overrides. Verify precedence against the current Epic documentation before making them engine-authoritative.

## Settings precedence requirement

For any sensitive behavior, the final technical documentation should say whether the authority is:

1. Island Settings baseline
2. Native device override
3. Engine global configuration
4. Game Mode configuration
5. Match runtime state

Do not leave precedence implicit.

## Critical settings to inspect

- Max Players
- Join In Progress
- Spawn behavior
- Spawn immunity
- Spawn limits
- After Last Spawn Go To
- Post Game Spawn Location
- team assignment behavior
- score behavior
- rounds
- Team Settings & Inventory overrides
- Class Designer overrides

The current Epic documentation states that Join In Progress can be configured as Spawn on Next Round, Spawn, Spectate, or a team number; this must be reconciled with the engine's own JIP policy rather than assumed to be automatically overridden by Verse.


---

# Appendix B — Verbatim `UEFN_In_World_UMG_Widgets_Report(3).md`

# UEFN / Verse / Scene Graph / UMG — In-World User Widgets Technical Report

**Purpose:** Reference document for Google AI Studio and other coding assistants working on Unreal Editor for Fortnite (UEFN) projects.

**Scope:** UMG User Widgets used as **world-space / in-world widgets**, their Verse Fields, the generated Scene Graph entity representation, Scene Graph transforms/hierarchy, and the correct ways to create, place, modify, spawn, and remove these widgets with Verse.

**Research date:** August 30, 2026

**Primary authority:** Epic Games / Fortnite Developer Documentation. When this document conflicts with older tutorials, forum posts, generated code, or model memory, prefer the current Epic documentation and the actual project's generated Verse digest/API surface.

---

## 1. Executive Model

The most important concept is that an in-world UMG widget has **two closely related representations**:

1. **The UMG User Widget asset/class** — the UI design itself. This is authored in UMG. Its hierarchy contains Text Blocks, Images, Buttons, Panels, animations, etc. Verse Fields are defined here and can be bound to UMG properties/events through View Bindings.
2. **The Scene Graph entity representation** — the world-space object created from that User Widget. This representation can be placed into the level/prefabs or spawned/attached through Scene Graph Verse. It has entity hierarchy and can be manipulated through Scene Graph APIs such as transforms.

Epic explicitly states that each User Widget is represented in Verse as a class and that a corresponding Scene Graph entity exists for it. For example, a widget named `UW_Scoreboard` corresponds to `UW_Scoreboard_entity`. When modifying the behavior/placement of the widget **as a world entity**, Verse must target the entity class, not only the ordinary User Widget class.

### Mental model

```text
UMG User Widget Asset
        |
        |  UMG Designer defines appearance/layout/animations
        |  Verse Fields define Verse-facing data/events
        v
+----------------------------+
| UW_MyWidget                |  <- UMG/User Widget class
|                            |
| Text / Images / Panels ... |
| Verse Fields               |
| View Bindings              |
| UMG Animations             |
+----------------------------+
        |
        | generated Scene Graph representation
        v
+----------------------------+
| UW_MyWidget_entity         |  <- world-space Scene Graph entity
|                            |
| Transform / parent/child   |
| Scene Graph components     |
| inherited widget behavior  |
+----------------------------+
        |
        | placed in level / prefab
        | or attached/spawned by Verse
        v
      WORLD
```

**Critical distinction:** changing the UMG asset changes the underlying widget design. Changing a particular `_entity` instance's transform or Scene Graph hierarchy changes that world instance. The two operations should not be treated as interchangeable.

Epic's in-world widget documentation:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/inworld-user-widgets-using-scene-graph-in-fortnite

Epic's 41.20 release notes, when in-world UMG Widgets were introduced:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/41-20-fortnite-ecosystem-updates-and-release-notes-in-fortnite

---

# 2. What an In-World UMG Widget Actually Is

An in-world widget is **still a UMG User Widget**. It is not a totally different UI technology and it does not require rebuilding the visual UI in Verse UI.

The difference is where the User Widget is represented/rendered:

- A normal screen-space User Widget is generally added to a player's UI/HUD.
- An in-world User Widget is represented as a Scene Graph entity and exists at a world location/orientation/scale.

Epic's 41.20 release notes state that a UMG User Widget can be dragged from the Content Browser into the viewport to display its UI in the level, or dragged into the Prefab Editor as part of an entity prefab. Existing UMG functionality carries over, including Verse Fields and UI animations. The widget is reflected as an entity subclass using the `[WidgetName]_entity` naming form.

This means the correct architecture is **UMG for presentation + Verse Fields for data/event exposure + Scene Graph entity for world placement and world hierarchy**.

---

# 3. UMG User Widget: The Design Layer

The UMG User Widget is authored using the UEFN UI Widget Editor.

A User Widget can contain:

- Containers such as Canvas, Overlay, Stack Box, Grid, Uniform Grid, Size Box, Scale Box, Scroll Box, etc.
- Elements such as Text Blocks, Images, Materials, and button widgets.
- Nested User Widgets.
- UMG animations.
- Verse Fields.
- View Bindings connecting Verse Fields with widget properties or widget events.

Epic recommends compartmentalizing UI into individual User Widgets and layering those widgets under parent widgets for complex UI systems. That same modularity remains valuable for world-space widgets.

UMG layout is still the responsibility of the UMG hierarchy. Scene Graph should not be used to replace ordinary UMG layout operations such as placing a text label 20 pixels to the right of an image. Scene Graph should be used for the **world-space placement and hierarchy of the complete widget entity**.

Useful Epic references:

- UI Widget Editor: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/ui-widget-editor-in-unreal-editor-for-fortnite
- UI Layout in UMG: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/ui-layout-in-umg-in-unreal-editor-for-fortnite
- Widget Types: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/widget-types-in-unreal-editor-for-fortnite

---

# 4. Verse Fields in UMG

Verse Fields are the bridge between the UMG asset and Verse logic.

Epic introduced Verse Fields in UMG in Fortnite v38.00. They allow developers to define variables in the UMG Designer, bind those variables to widget properties through View Bindings, and then expose/use the variables from Verse. The release notes specifically list field types including:

- `logic`
- `int`
- `float`
- `message`
- `material`
- `texture`

Verse Fields are reflected into the Verse asset digest for the User Widget. This is important because a coding assistant should not guess the names/types of fields: it should inspect the project's generated digest/compiler information when possible.

Source:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/fortnite/38-00-fortnite-ecosystem-updates-and-release-notes

---

## 4.1 Data flow: Verse -> UMG

The common pattern is:

```text
Gameplay/system state
        |
        v
Verse variable/value
        |
        | set Widget.SomeField
        v
UMG Verse Field
        |
        | View Binding
        v
UMG widget property
        |
        v
Visible UI
```

For example, conceptually:

```verse
set ScoreboardWidget.MyMessage = MyMessage
```

The field `MyMessage` exists on the User Widget, and the UMG widget property is bound to that field through the UMG View Bindings system.

The code is not directly finding a `TextBlock` in the widget tree and mutating arbitrary UMG internals. The intended Verse Fields workflow is to expose the data the widget needs and bind the data to the presentation in UMG.

This separation is especially useful for a world widget because the same visual widget can be placed on many world entities while different Verse logic supplies different field values.

---

# 5. Verse Fields: Events and Data Coming Back From UMG

Verse Fields are not limited to one-way data anymore.

Fortnite v39.40 introduced the **Verse field event type** in UMG. A Verse Field event can be bound to a widget event through View Bindings, allowing Verse to react to user/UI events such as a button interaction.

Fortnite v40.20 expanded event fields to support a single parameter of type:

- `float`
- `int`
- `logic`

This allows UMG to send both an event and a value back to Verse.

Example conceptual flow:

```text
Player/UI interaction
        |
        v
UMG widget event
        |
        | View Binding
        v
Verse Field event
        |
        v
Verse handler
        |
        v
Game logic
```

For parameterized events:

```text
UMG interaction
    -> Verse Field Event(int)
    -> Verse awaits/subscribes according to generated API
    -> Verse receives the integer
```

The exact generated field/event signature should be taken from the project's current Verse digest rather than inferred from old examples.

Sources:

- v39.40: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/39-40-fortnite-ecosystem-updates-and-release-notes
- v40.20: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/40-20-fortnite-ecosystem-updates-and-release-notes

---

# 6. View Bindings: Why They Matter

View Bindings are the connection layer inside UMG.

A Verse Field by itself is not automatically the visible text, texture, material, visibility state, animation trigger, etc. The UMG designer must bind the field to an appropriate widget property or event.

For a normal field:

```text
Verse Field: MyMessage
        |
        | View Binding
        v
Text Block: Text
```

For a material/texture field:

```text
Verse Field: MyTexture
        |
        | View Binding
        v
Image: Brush / image property
```

For an event:

```text
Button: OnClicked
        |
        | View Binding
        v
Verse Field Event: CloseEvent
```

The UMG asset therefore contains the actual UI wiring. Verse supplies or consumes the data/events.

This distinction matters when troubleshooting. If Verse successfully changes a field but the screen does not change, the first suspicion should be the UMG field/view-binding configuration, not the Scene Graph transform.

Epic Custom Buttons example:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/custom-buttons-in-fortnite

---

# 7. The `_entity` Representation

For every existing User Widget that supports the in-world workflow, UEFN exposes a corresponding Scene Graph entity representation.

Example:

```text
UMG User Widget:
UW_Scoreboard

Scene Graph entity:
UW_Scoreboard_entity
```

Epic explicitly warns that when modifying the behavior of the widget entity, Verse must access the **entity class**, not only the widget class.

That distinction should be treated as a hard rule by an AI coding assistant:

> **If the task concerns world-space placement, hierarchy, spawning, parenting, transforms, or Scene Graph behavior, use the `[WidgetName]_entity` representation.**
>
> **If the task concerns UI appearance/data exposed through Verse Fields, use the User Widget's Verse Fields and UMG bindings.**

The generated exact namespace for an entity depends on the project's asset structure. Never hard-code a namespace from an unrelated tutorial when the project's generated digest shows a different one.

---

# 8. How to Place an In-World Widget Manually

Epic supports directly dragging an existing UMG User Widget Blueprint from the Content Browser into the level. UEFN creates the corresponding entity representation in the scene.

Basic workflow:

1. Create/design the User Widget in UMG.
2. Add any Verse Fields required for dynamic data.
3. Create View Bindings between those fields and the UI properties/events.
4. Compile/save the widget.
5. Drag the User Widget from the Content Browser into the level.
6. Treat the resulting object as a Scene Graph entity.
7. Adjust its world-space position, orientation, and scale using Scene Graph/transform controls.

The widget is now a world-space object rather than simply a player's HUD widget.

Epic reference:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/inworld-user-widgets-using-scene-graph-in-fortnite

---

# 9. Adding a Widget Under an Existing Entity

A blank Scene Graph entity can be used as a parent, and the User Widget entity can be added beneath it.

Conceptually:

```text
World Entity / Object
    |
    +-- UW_Nameplate_entity
    |
    +-- UW_HealthBar_entity
    |
    +-- UW_Status_entity
```

This is often the preferred design for a world object that has multiple UI elements or other components.

Parenting is significant because Scene Graph entities are hierarchical. The parent controls the lifetime of child entities; removing the parent from the scene removes its children as well.

This also means that a widget can inherit world-space movement/rotation from its parent. A nameplate can therefore move with a character/object by becoming a child of an appropriate Scene Graph entity.

Epic Scene Graph entity API:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/verse-api/versedotorg/scenegraph/entity

---

# 10. Spawning / Attaching a Widget with Verse

Epic documents adding an existing User Widget entity to another entity using Verse.

The general pattern is:

```verse
using { /Verse.org/SceneGraph }

inworld_ui_spawner_component<public> := class<final_super>(component):
    WidgetToSpawn : UW_MyWidget_entity = UW_MyWidget_entity{}
```

The entity can then be added to a target entity's hierarchy using Scene Graph entity operations.

The important conceptual operation is:

```text
TargetEntity.AddEntities(array{WidgetEntity})
```

`AddEntities` makes the provided entity/entities children of the target entity. If the child already has a parent, Scene Graph removes it from the current parent and re-parents it to the new parent.

Epic entity API:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/verse-api/versedotorg/scenegraph/entity

Epic in-world widget example:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/inworld-user-widgets-using-scene-graph-in-fortnite

---

# 11. Removing a World Widget

Because an in-world widget is a Scene Graph entity, removal is an entity operation.

The entity API exposes `RemoveFromParent`.

Conceptually:

```verse
WidgetEntity.RemoveFromParent()
```

This removes the widget from its parent and therefore removes it from the active entity hierarchy/scene. The parent controls child lifetime.

The distinction is important:

```text
Screen-space widget:
    Player UI -> RemoveWidget(...)

World-space widget:
    Scene Graph entity -> RemoveFromParent()
```

Do not make an AI model assume that `player_ui.RemoveWidget` is the correct mechanism for an in-world Scene Graph widget.

Epic entity API:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/verse-api/versedotorg/scenegraph/entity

For conventional player UI creation/removal, see:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/fortnite/creating-and-removing-widgets-in-unreal-editor-for-fortnite

---

# 12. Scene Graph Transforms: Location, Rotation, Scale

An in-world widget is a physical world-space entity, so transform handling is a major part of using it correctly.

Scene Graph transforms contain:

- Translation/location
- Rotation/orientation
- Scale/size

The relevant Scene Graph concepts are:

```text
transform
    Translation
    Rotation
    Scale

transform_component
    LocalTransform
    optional Origin
```

Epic recommends using entity extension methods such as:

```verse
Entity.SetLocalTransform(MyTransform)
Entity.SetGlobalTransform(MyTransform)
Entity.GetLocalTransform()
Entity.GetGlobalTransform()
```

These are preferred over manually retrieving and manipulating the `transform_component` for common transform operations.

Epic notes that `SetLocalTransform` and `SetGlobalTransform` will create a transform component when one does not already exist.

Important distinction:

- **Local transform** = relative to the entity's parent/origin.
- **Global transform** = relative to the world origin.

For a widget parented to a character/object, local transform is usually the appropriate way to define its offset from the parent.

Epic transform documentation:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/transforms-in-scene-graph-in-unreal-editor-for-fortnite

Epic `SetGlobalTransform`:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/verse-api/versedotorg/scenegraph/setglobaltransform

Epic `GetGlobalTransform`:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/verse-api/versedotorg/scenegraph/getglobaltransform

---

# 13. Local vs Global Placement Example

Suppose the entity hierarchy is:

```text
EnemyEntity
    |
    +-- UW_EnemyNameplate_entity
```

If the nameplate should remain above the enemy when the enemy moves, use the child entity's local transform.

Conceptually:

```verse
Nameplate.SetLocalTransform(
    transform{
        Translation := vector3{
            Left := 0.0,
            Up := 0.0,
            Forward := 200.0
        }
    }
)
```

The exact coordinate values and axis meanings must be verified against the project's coordinate convention and desired orientation. Scene Graph uses the Verse SpatialMath system; do not copy transform code from an older API without checking its imports and current type definitions.

Epic SpatialMath reference:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/verse-api/unrealenginedotcom/temporary/spatialmath

Epic transform reference:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/transforms-in-scene-graph-in-unreal-editor-for-fortnite

---

# 14. World Widget Size Is Not the Same as UMG Pixel Size

A common source of confusion is that a UMG design is authored in UI/layout space, while an in-world widget is rendered as a physical object in the world.

Epic's in-world widget troubleshooting guidance specifically says that a widget can appear too small, particularly when it only contains a small amount of text or a small image. The widget's world bounds conform closely to its content. Epic recommends temporarily scaling the entity up (approximately 10x) to make it visible, then fine-tuning the scale.

Therefore:

```text
UMG layout size != final perceived world size
```

The UMG widget may be perfectly designed while the world entity is physically too small.

Troubleshooting also includes:

- Widget placed below the ground.
- Widget too small.
- Widget facing an unexpected direction.

Epic in-world widget documentation:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/inworld-user-widgets-using-scene-graph-in-fortnite

---

# 15. Orientation / Facing Direction

In-world widgets occupy a 3D world location. Therefore, unlike screen-space UI, the player can observe them from different directions.

A widget can technically exist at the correct coordinates while still looking invisible because its front face is oriented away from the player.

Debugging order:

1. Verify it exists in the level/entity hierarchy.
2. Verify its global location is reasonable.
3. Verify its scale is large enough to see.
4. Rotate it to a known orientation.
5. Move the player around it to confirm which side is the visible side.
6. Only then debug UMG itself.

Do not immediately rewrite the widget when the actual problem is a world transform.

---

# 16. Animations Carry Over to the World Widget

Epic explicitly states that existing UMG functionality carries over to in-world entities, including UI animations and Verse Fields.

That means the UMG asset remains the correct place to design an animation such as:

- Fade in/out
- Pop/scale
- Damage indicator
- Status change
- Value-change animation
- Material/texture animation

Verse can then drive the relevant exposed field/binding or animation workflow.

Epic's UI animation documentation uses Sequencer/UMG animation workflows and describes animation driven by properties such as float/int variables.

Reference:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/fortnite/aninmating-ui

---

# 17. In-World Widgets Are Not Equivalent to HUD Widgets

This distinction must be preserved.

## HUD / Screen-space

A standard player UI workflow associates custom UI with a specific player. Epic describes custom UI as player-specific: a custom UI is associated with a player and only that player sees it.

Typical architecture:

```text
player
  |
  +-- player_ui
        |
        +-- User Widget
```

Reference:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/fortnite/ingame-user-interfaces-in-unreal-editor-for-fortnite

## In-world

The widget is represented by a Scene Graph entity in the world.

Typical architecture:

```text
Scene Graph
   |
   +-- WorldEntity
          |
          +-- UW_MyWidget_entity
```

The widget therefore has physical world placement and can be parented to another Scene Graph entity.

Epic's in-world documentation specifically describes world widgets as Scene Graph entities and notes that they are not directly compatible with standard Creative devices; device functionality must be connected through Verse devices/custom Verse logic.

---

# 18. Do Not Confuse UMG with Verse UI

UEFN has multiple UI creation paths.

### UMG

UMG is the visual editor/workflow for User Widgets and is especially appropriate when designers need a reusable visual asset.

### Verse UI

Verse can construct UI programmatically using types such as `canvas`, `text_block`, `button`, etc.

### In-world UMG

In-world widgets in this document specifically refer to the newer workflow where a **UMG User Widget is represented as a Scene Graph entity**.

It is therefore incorrect to replace an in-world UMG widget with a Verse `canvas` simply because both are called UI.

The question being solved is specifically:

```text
UMG User Widget
    + Verse Fields
    + View Bindings
    + Scene Graph entity representation
    = In-world UMG Widget
```

---

# 19. Reusable Widget vs Widget Instance

A critical architecture rule is to distinguish **asset/class-level configuration** from **instance-level state**.

## Asset/class-level

Owned by the User Widget design:

- Widget hierarchy
- Text/image layout
- Fonts/styles
- Default field configuration
- View Bindings
- UMG animations
- Which child widgets exist
- Which Verse Fields/events are exposed

Changing these generally changes every use of that widget asset.

## Instance/entity-level

Owned by the Scene Graph entity instance:

- World position
- World rotation
- World scale
- Parent entity
- Scene Graph component structure
- Runtime world hierarchy
- Which specific entity instance gets which gameplay data

This is the equivalent of:

```text
Widget asset = reusable class/design
Widget entity = one placed instance of that design
```

An AI coding assistant should determine which layer the requested change belongs to before writing code.

---

# 20. Recommended Architecture for Dynamic World UI

For a dynamic world UI such as a nameplate, health bar, objective marker, scoreboard, terminal display, floating interaction information, or status indicator, use this pattern:

```text
                         GAMEPLAY
                            |
                            v
                     Verse gameplay logic
                            |
             +--------------+--------------+
             |                             |
             v                             v
       World/entity state            Widget data
             |                             |
             v                             v
      Scene Graph entity          UMG Verse Fields
             |                             |
             |                             v
             |                       View Bindings
             |                             |
             +----------------------> UMG visuals
```

If the UI belongs to a specific physical object:

```text
ObjectEntity
    |
    +-- Mesh/components/etc.
    |
    +-- UW_ObjectNameplate_entity
    |
    +-- UW_ObjectHealth_entity
```

Each widget can receive different data through its exposed Verse Fields.

---

# 21. Example: Dynamic World Nameplate

Suppose a project needs a floating nameplate above a world entity.

### UMG side

Create:

```text
UW_Nameplate
    Canvas/Overlay
        Text Block
```

Add a Verse Field:

```text
NameMessage : message
```

Bind:

```text
NameMessage -> Text Block.Text
```

### Scene Graph side

Use:

```text
UW_Nameplate_entity
```

as a child of the world object.

### Verse side

Conceptually:

```verse
ObjectEntity.AddEntities(array{NameplateEntity})
set NameplateEntity.NameMessage = DisplayName
```

The exact generated entity/field syntax must be validated against the project's `Assets.digest.verse` and compiler output. The architectural idea is stable even when namespace names differ.

Result:

```text
Object moves
    -> child entity moves
        -> world nameplate moves

Game changes name
    -> Verse changes NameMessage
        -> UMG binding changes Text
```

This cleanly separates spatial behavior from visual data behavior.

---

# 22. Example: Dynamic World Health Bar

UMG:

```text
UW_HealthBar
    Background Image
    Fill Image
```

Expose a numeric Verse Field, for example:

```text
HealthPercent : float
```

Bind the field to the appropriate UMG property/material parameter used by the health bar.

Scene Graph:

```text
CharacterEntity
    |
    +-- UW_HealthBar_entity
```

Verse:

```text
Character health changes
        |
        v
Calculate health percentage
        |
        v
set HealthBarEntity.HealthPercent = Value
        |
        v
UMG binding updates the visible bar
```

The world transform and the value update are separate concerns.

---

# 23. Multiple Instances of the Same Widget

A major benefit of this architecture is reuse.

One User Widget asset can conceptually be used as:

```text
UW_Nameplate
    |
    +-- UW_Nameplate_entity for Enemy A
    +-- UW_Nameplate_entity for Enemy B
    +-- UW_Nameplate_entity for Enemy C
```

Each entity instance can have a different world transform and can be supplied different Verse Field values.

Do not create three visually identical UMG assets solely because the three instances need different names, colors, health values, etc. Those are data differences and should generally be represented through exposed Verse Fields/bindings.

---

# 24. Parenting Strategy

If a widget should track another object, prefer hierarchy rather than repeatedly recalculating global coordinates when possible.

Good pattern:

```text
EnemyEntity
    |
    +-- UIAnchorEntity
           |
           +-- UW_Nameplate_entity
```

Possible advantages:

- Parent movement naturally moves the widget.
- A common offset can be expressed as a local transform.
- Multiple world-space widgets can share an anchor.
- Runtime object cleanup can remove child widgets through normal Scene Graph lifetime behavior.

However, the correct hierarchy depends on the game's architecture. Do not blindly parent every widget to an entity if the desired behavior is actually screen-relative or player-relative.

---

# 25. Entity Lifetime and Removal

Scene Graph is hierarchical. The parent controls the lifetime of its children.

Epic's entity API states that when an entity is removed from the scene, its child entities and components are removed as well.

This is useful for UI cleanup:

```text
EnemyEntity removed
    |
    +-- Nameplate removed
    +-- Health bar removed
    +-- Status UI removed
```

This can be safer than managing separate cleanup systems for every child widget, provided the hierarchy is intentionally designed that way.

---

# 26. Scene Graph Entity Mutation

The Scene Graph entity API allows the structure and content of entities to be changed dynamically.

Relevant operations include:

- `GetParent`
- `AddEntities`
- `RemoveFromParent`
- `GetEntities`
- `AddComponents`
- `GetComponent`
- `GetComponents`

`GetEntities()` returns direct child entities accessible from the calling context. It does not recursively return every descendant. For deeper searches, Epic provides Scene Graph query functionality.

This matters when writing an AI-generated controller. It should not assume `GetEntities()` recursively finds a deeply nested widget.

Reference:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/verse-api/versedotorg/scenegraph/entity

---

# 27. Asset Digest: Source of Truth for Generated Widget APIs

A User Widget's Verse-facing fields are reflected into the Verse asset digest.

This is one of the most important mechanisms for reliable AI-assisted UEFN development.

The coding assistant should treat these as authoritative:

1. Current project's `Assets.digest.verse` / generated Verse asset definitions.
2. Current compiler diagnostics.
3. Current Epic Verse API documentation.
4. Current UEFN editor state.

It should not invent a field name such as `Text`, `Message`, `Value`, or `Health` merely because those names are common.

Likewise, it should not assume that every User Widget gets the same namespace. UEFN project asset paths affect generated symbol names.

The correct workflow is:

```text
User Widget created
        |
        v
Verse Fields configured
        |
        v
Compile/build
        |
        v
Generated digest exposes fields/entity
        |
        v
Verse references actual generated symbol
```

---

# 28. Important Compatibility Rule: Standard Devices vs Scene Graph

Epic's Scene Graph documentation states that Scene Graph entities/components/prefabs are not directly compatible with standard Creative devices. They can be used on the same island, but custom Verse code is required when connecting their functionality.

Therefore, an AI model should not assume that an in-world widget entity can simply be assigned to an arbitrary device property that expects a traditional Creative device or HUD widget.

Correct pattern:

```text
Creative Device event
        |
        v
Verse device/controller
        |
        v
Scene Graph entity / widget entity
```

Reference:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/getting-started-in-scene-graph-in-fortnite

---

# 29. Interaction Limitation

Epic's in-world widget documentation currently states that you cannot interact directly with in-world UI created with widgets. The intended use described there is UI that reacts to in-game events, such as a score increase or health loss.

This needs to be distinguished from newer **tappable HUD widgets**, which are specifically a screen-space custom HUD workflow. The 41.10 documentation describes touchscreen/gamepad/keyboard interaction for custom HUD widgets using Custom Button or Verse Button workflows.

Do not infer that the existence of tappable HUD widgets means an in-world UMG Scene Graph entity automatically supports direct player click/tap interaction.

References:

- In-world UMG: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/inworld-user-widgets-using-scene-graph-in-fortnite
- Tappable HUD Widgets: https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/tappable-custom-hud-widgets-in-fortnite

---

# 30. Common Mistakes an AI Assistant Must Avoid

## Mistake 1: Treating `_entity` and the User Widget class as identical

Incorrect mental model:

```text
UW_Widget == UW_Widget_entity
```

Correct:

```text
UW_Widget = UMG widget class/design
UW_Widget_entity = Scene Graph entity representation
```

---

## Mistake 2: Using `player_ui.AddWidget` for an in-world Scene Graph widget

`player_ui.AddWidget` is the screen-space/player UI workflow.

For an in-world widget, use the Scene Graph entity representation and entity hierarchy.

---

## Mistake 3: Rebuilding a UMG widget entirely in Verse UI

If the requirement is specifically an in-world UMG User Widget, keep the UI design in UMG and expose required data/events through Verse Fields.

---

## Mistake 4: Directly searching the UMG tree from Verse for ordinary data updates

Use exposed Verse Fields + View Bindings as the intended bridge for dynamic widget data wherever applicable.

---

## Mistake 5: Changing a global asset when only one instance should change

Changing the UMG asset/layout affects the reusable widget design. Changing a Scene Graph entity's transform affects the individual world instance.

---

## Mistake 6: Confusing layout scale with world scale

UMG's internal layout size and a Scene Graph entity's world scale are different layers.

---

## Mistake 7: Assuming `GetEntities()` is recursive

Epic documents `GetEntities()` as returning direct children only.

---

## Mistake 8: Guessing generated field names or namespaces

Use the project's generated digest and compiler output.

---

## Mistake 9: Using global transforms when local hierarchy is intended

If a widget is a child of the object it follows, local transform is often the appropriate representation for its offset.

---

## Mistake 10: Assuming HUD input behavior applies to world widgets

Tappable HUD widgets are a separate, screen-space workflow.

---

# 31. Troubleshooting Decision Tree

When an in-world widget does not appear:

```text
Does the entity exist in the Scene Graph / level?
        |
       NO -> Fix placement/spawn/parenting/entity creation.
        |
       YES
        v
Is it in a sensible world location?
        |
       NO -> Fix global/local transform.
        |
       YES
        v
Is its world scale large enough?
        |
       NO -> Increase entity scale temporarily.
        |
       YES
        v
Is it facing a visible direction?
        |
       NO -> Fix rotation/orientation.
        |
       YES
        v
Does the UMG asset render by itself?
        |
       NO -> Fix UMG hierarchy/layout/assets.
        |
       YES
        v
Are Verse Fields bound correctly?
        |
       NO -> Fix UMG Verse Field / View Binding.
        |
       YES
        v
Does Verse use the current generated field/entity type?
        |
       NO -> Fix symbol/namespace/type from digest.
        |
       YES
        v
Check runtime events/data flow/compiler errors.
```

Epic's own troubleshooting specifically calls out below-ground placement, very small widgets, and incorrect orientation.

---

# 32. Recommended Development Workflow

For a production UEFN project, use this workflow for every new world-space widget:

### Phase A — UMG design

1. Create the User Widget.
2. Build the visual hierarchy.
3. Create reusable child widgets where appropriate.
4. Add UMG animations.
5. Add Verse Fields for values that must be controlled by Verse.
6. Add Verse event fields for interactions that need to communicate back to Verse.
7. Configure View Bindings.
8. Compile/save.

### Phase B — Scene Graph

1. Use the generated `_entity` class.
2. Place it directly in the level or put it under an entity/prefab.
3. Establish parent/child hierarchy intentionally.
4. Set local transform for relative offsets.
5. Use global transform when absolute world placement is actually required.

### Phase C — Runtime Verse

1. Reference the correct generated entity/field types.
2. Attach/spawn/reparent with Scene Graph entity operations.
3. Feed gameplay values into Verse Fields.
4. React to Verse Field events when needed.
5. Remove the entity through Scene Graph lifecycle operations when no longer needed.

### Phase D — Validation

1. Verify compile.
2. Inspect the generated digest.
3. Launch a session.
4. Check world transform.
5. Check scale/orientation.
6. Check field binding/data.
7. Check runtime lifetime/parenting.

---

# 33. Architecture Rules for Google AI Studio

The following rules should be treated as hard constraints when generating or modifying code for an existing UEFN project:

### Rule A — Identify the layer first

Before modifying code, determine whether the request concerns:

```text
UMG design/layout
Verse Fields / View Bindings
Scene Graph entity hierarchy
Scene Graph transforms
Runtime Verse gameplay/data
Player HUD / screen-space UI
```

Do not use an API from another layer merely because it seems similar.

### Rule B — World widget = UMG + entity

Always model an in-world UMG widget as two representations of one UI asset:

```text
User Widget class
+
Scene Graph `_entity` class/instance
```

### Rule C — Use the entity for world operations

For:

- position
- rotation
- scale
- parenting
- spawning/attaching
- removal
- Scene Graph components

use the Scene Graph entity representation.

### Rule D — Use Verse Fields for designed data flow

For:

- displayed text
- numeric values
- textures
- materials
- visibility/state where exposed
- animation triggers
- widget event communication

prefer the User Widget's Verse Fields and View Bindings.

### Rule E — Do not invent APIs

Before writing code, check the project's generated Verse digest and current Epic API documentation.

### Rule F — Respect current UEFN version

In-world UMG is a relatively new feature (introduced in Fortnite v41.20). Older UEFN tutorials pre-dating v41.20 may not describe the current world-widget workflow.

### Rule G — Do not assume device compatibility

Scene Graph entities are not directly standard-device-compatible. Use Verse to connect traditional device events/logic to Scene Graph entities where required.

### Rule H — Separate asset state from instance state

Never make a global UMG asset modification when the desired change is only for one entity instance. Conversely, do not add duplicated runtime transform logic when the desired behavior is a reusable layout change.

---

# 34. Version History Relevant to This System

## v38.00 — Verse Fields in UMG

UMG gained Verse Fields allowing Verse to drive widget data, materials, animations, and properties through View Bindings. Fields became visible in the Verse asset digest.

Source:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/fortnite/38-00-fortnite-ecosystem-updates-and-release-notes

## v39.40 — Verse Field Events

UMG Verse Fields gained an event type so UI actions could generate events handled from Verse.

Source:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/39-40-fortnite-ecosystem-updates-and-release-notes

## v40.20 — Parameters on Verse Field Events

Events gained a single `float`, `int`, or `logic` parameter, allowing UI interactions to send values to Verse.

Source:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/40-20-fortnite-ecosystem-updates-and-release-notes

## v41.20 — In-World UMG Widgets

UMG User Widgets became usable directly as world-space Scene Graph entities. Widgets can be dragged into the level or prefab editor, and the `_entity` representation was introduced for Verse/world placement. UMG Verse Fields and animations carry over to the in-world entity.

Source:  
https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/fortnite/41-20-fortnite-ecosystem-updates-and-release-notes-in-fortnite

# 36. Final Technical Summary

The correct mental model is:

```text
                         UMG
                          |
                 User Widget Asset
                          |
            +-------------+-------------+
            |                           |
       Verse Fields                UMG visual tree
            |                           |
       View Bindings                animations
            |
            +-------------+
                          |
                          v
               Verse-accessible widget
                          |
                          v
               `_entity` representation
                          |
              Scene Graph hierarchy
                          |
                 world transform
                          |
                          v
                      WORLD
```

For an AI coding assistant, the decisive rule is:

> **UMG defines what the widget looks like and exposes its data/events. Scene Graph defines where the widget instance exists and how it relates to other world entities. Verse connects gameplay state to the widget fields and controls the entity hierarchy/transform at runtime.**

An in-world UMG widget is therefore **not merely a HUD widget moved into the world**. It is a UMG User Widget that also has a Scene Graph entity representation, allowing the UI to participate in the world/entity hierarchy while retaining UMG features such as Verse Fields and animations.

When in doubt, inspect the generated `Assets.digest.verse` and current compiler/API information before inventing a symbol, namespace, field type, or method.

   ## **1\. Core Language Fundamentals**

   ### **Syntax Rules**

- The set Keyword: Unlike C++, you cannot simply write x \= 5\. You must use set x \= 5\.  
- Failure Contexts: Array indexing Array\[0\] or Type Casting int(MyFloat) are "failable." They must be wrapped in an if or for block.  
- Specifiers:  
  * \<public\>, \<private\>, \<internal\>, \<protected\>: Scope control.\[[1](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFXONv2InK8szXgpQKvnGQAuUMAnO6uWhBmc2_gvxfe1zslKxXw-F7CKH4GZpVuFNnc9d6clcPivgphUbjKEFio1CRTO8GEcbD1rHQHlQqsifksYx_B6nD7Vh37P20s8f8=)\]  
  * \<final\>: Prevents subclassing.  
  * \<abstract\>: Class cannot be instantiated.\[[2](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQHd-hRNXrhwsvOmE13xcVekC0hvGanZ_XFW13LYIKmH3mjYjdaKrhqNDlV8w7anQJWlF7F_ox8_iLaKcESSyVoPUpPBWiPMeZnju6-fgNMhqPvhaonMAhzBvSY0ZIEA92NU8Lfyenp9c-we3xUYinN7FE5ef4PQMKxivbqoerLY)\]  
    

  ### **Effect System**

* ***\<suspends\>***: Required for any function using Sleep() or Await().  
* ***\<decides\>***: Required for functions that can fail and return control to the failure context.  
* ***\<transacts\>***: Required if the function modifies data that might need to revert upon failure.  
  ---

  ## **2\. The Verse API (2026 Standards)**

  ### **Essential Imports**

* *using { /Verse.org/Simulation }*  
* *using { /Verse.org/Assets }*

* *using { /Fortnite.com/Characters }*  
* *using { /Fortnite.com/Playspaces }*  
* *using { /UnrealEngine.com/Temporary/Diagnostics }*  
* *using { /UnrealEngine.com/Temporary/SpatialMath }*


  ### **New 2026 Modules**

  ## **3\. The Scene Graph System (Entities & Components)**

  As of late 2025, UEFN shifted toward an Entity-Component System (ECS).  
* Entity: The base object.\[[4](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQH3aZ0n1HNnyno24mhla94L2KE5Qc2ZCK2LjXAsLWlpkgJxZiZSeIq2Es764WIIp26SIkARpr52uonIqhtxDxbvhryxbZ8LuWihSmkbUtXGO8z1zM5Xo2gzvZmgm90TjsYoI282rHbCLeh7PKhuyQ9O1zaO3ZKQcuyfdE0xpLspK_C_GjA1E_DZNBhlKUm-VQ807QR--4QLbg==)\] Use GetParent() and AddEntities().\[[4](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQH3aZ0n1HNnyno24mhla94L2KE5Qc2ZCK2LjXAsLWlpkgJxZiZSeIq2Es764WIIp26SIkARpr52uonIqhtxDxbvhryxbZ8LuWihSmkbUtXGO8z1zM5Xo2gzvZmgm90TjsYoI282rHbCLeh7PKhuyQ9O1zaO3ZKQcuyfdE0xpLspK_C_GjA1E_DZNBhlKUm-VQ807QR--4QLbg==)\]  
* Component: Where logic lives.\[[4](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQH3aZ0n1HNnyno24mhla94L2KE5Qc2ZCK2LjXAsLWlpkgJxZiZSeIq2Es764WIIp26SIkARpr52uonIqhtxDxbvhryxbZ8LuWihSmkbUtXGO8z1zM5Xo2gzvZmgm90TjsYoI282rHbCLeh7PKhuyQ9O1zaO3ZKQcuyfdE0xpLspK_C_GjA1E_DZNBhlKUm-VQ807QR--4QLbg==)\]\[[5](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQE3E7VzR0AhzES47LhUxcyZDZMMOTVG4CNFyoXFVXrHMDUINIOgTSR5m8wP99zidK3u5dhPU1asDppAmmUeFL6f5afqigCjghnx1V1lgR5rv2pZqzNeVBFsw1SXBnE1mEDPbdvnlZORnbJsBd43DlDQcKwH6HwsHft8ZmzpNzMmJ5bL_8hm0uX864AaZVWyxck4huP7-uMw0UkFkP5rKHijsFREEhEzqiU=)\]\[[6](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQHTm4ejrD_0-M_ubDwS-m0YIt1-GIV8xfbp7xR10BNzBdDmr5e9KKawvgC47dvkIZm4pG4USGASfagYIojTJFKLuA0Vn85i5QXja53721udI5XReIVjqXPFCScuGFJGJIkgw8VCoR9m72d15cgNd9_K6g65p8I8BTY17_QGyPZG2wjDjw6AxxwYKSldwY_yjXhE-ppp0yKXBN-LhCmyjrlxRWCwnZg=)\]\[[7](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQFuLKrKUqFhF26X-bPejUCTVkAnQhIVuFtoBoisQ-6r3egp8WpVdNLZvlvqz8v5Mer4cFLvV__6nKtzfIs0b3St3J6A-P5AhLmN2BMWg5OmQvAf24br--JzDOMOZAFBAv2iAbmgNw==)\] Inherit from component and use \<final\_super\>.  
* Prefabs: These are essentially entities with pre-defined components.\[[4](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQH3aZ0n1HNnyno24mhla94L2KE5Qc2ZCK2LjXAsLWlpkgJxZiZSeIq2Es764WIIp26SIkARpr52uonIqhtxDxbvhryxbZ8LuWihSmkbUtXGO8z1zM5Xo2gzvZmgm90TjsYoI282rHbCLeh7PKhuyQ9O1zaO3ZKQcuyfdE0xpLspK_C_GjA1E_DZNBhlKUm-VQ807QR--4QLbg==)\]\[[8](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQHOCv-vu23CtN5AWe_6RZZKV_peVT3rLf0kkPznutjuHJVJZ7r1eVkqT82VCHrvZY0X13A5AyvuYmFRdQVpGOv-Yzhq8kzxAykXsjAWipZcygyOlufxcrsLXyYW_TxIJ3AaymwtrfdYZ0B71-rTHLdTSwrL-5IbXB8MOcdPgOrjsX6eZ8C86lZzr8ya7b7Bpdw=)\]


  ## **The "Migration" Pattern:**

  Instead of putting all logic in a creative\_device, create a component and attach it to an Entity. This allows you to move logic dynamically in the world without being tethered to a physical device location.  
  ---

  ## **4\. Itemization & Inventory**

  ### **Custom Items**

* item\_component: Required for an entity to exist in an inventory.  
* inventory\_component: Attached to players or chests to hold items.  
* API Pattern:


  if (Inv := Agent.GetInventoryComponent\[\]):

  Inv.AddItem(MyCustomItem)

  ---

  ## **5\. Data Persistence**

  ### **The *weak\_map* Pattern**

  Persistence is stored per-player using a module-scoped (global) weak\_map.

*var PlayerDataMap : weak\_map(player, player\_data) \= map{}*

### **Versioning (The Option Pattern)**

To avoid losing data when you update your game, use optional fields for versioning:  
*player\_data := class\<persistable\>\<final\>:*  
*V1: ?player\_data\_v1 \= false*  
*V2: ?player\_data\_v2 \= false*

When migrating from V1 to V2, write a "Converter" function that reads the V1 option, populates V2, and then sets V1 to false to save memory.  
---

## **6\. The "Creative Workarounds" Library**

This section covers unconventional methods to bypass engine limitations.

### **A. The "Giant Monster" Scale Fix**

**Problem:** Fortnite characters cannot be scaled up.  
**Workaround:** Conceal the actual player model (make it invisible). Spawn a Large Static Mesh/Skeletal Mesh and parent it to the player entity. Use Verse to sync the animations/transforms of the large mesh to the player's inputs.

### **B. The "Pure Class" Entry Point**

**Problem:** Having 100+ creative\_device actors lags the game.  
**Workaround:** Use a single "Master Device" to instantiate "Pure Verse Classes."

codeVerse

\# A class that doesn't need to be placed in the world  
my\_logic\_class := class:  
    OnBegin():void \= Print("Logic Running")

\# Master Device  
master\_device := class(creative\_device):  
    OnBegin\<override\>()\<suspends\>:void \=  
        Logic := my\_logic\_class{}

        Logic.OnBegin()

### **C. The Bridge Device (Event Caller)**

**Problem:** Calling Verse functions from non-Verse systems.  
**Workaround:** Use a trigger\_device as a "Function Bridge." Bind the Verse function to the TriggeredEvent.\[[13](https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/grounding-api-redirect/AUZIYQGftqOfbEETFtv10f43qooaC0dDZDNfZKq44hm0H-ljEToygsWpNkDUtpjt6pix68sNbWi6PUpvGg-SvEN86ElqFMv6M87VlmyUJmc511ioteqNuNvJhsLSzjNzJvfcE-zG4Bm24ZrOGPlmAfY=)\] Now, any Sequencer, Button, or Tracker can "call" your Verse code by simply activating that trigger.

---

## **7\. Anti-Hallucination Checklist**

* **No new keyword.** (Correct: my\_class{})  
* **No semi-colons.**  
* **Indentation is 4 spaces.** (Verse is whitespace-sensitive).  
* **for loops use : not in.** (Correct: for (X : MyArray))  
* **set for all mutations.**  
  ---

AI<public> := module:

    equipped_sidekick_component<native><public> := class<final_super><epic_internal>(sidekick_component, showable):
        # By default, Sidekicks will change their mood depending on actions in the game.
        # This value will lock the Sidekick into the mood passed in, overriding the automatic mood system.
        var MoodOverride<override>:?sidekick_mood = external {}

        # Get the Sidekick's current mood.
        GetMood<override><native>()<reads>:sidekick_mood

        # Signaled whenever the Sidekick's mood changes, either via the underlying mood system, or an override is applied. Returns (Previous Mood, New Mood).
        ChangeMoodEvent<override><native>:listenable(tuple(sidekick_mood, sidekick_mood)) = external {}

        # Request to play a given reaction on the sidekick.
        # This reaction is not guaranteed to play immediately; instead, the StartPlayReactionEvent should be used to monitor this.
        # This will fail if the Sidekick cannot play the given reaction.
        PlayReaction<override><native>(Reaction:sidekick_reaction)<transacts><decides>:void

        # Signaled when the Sidekick starts to play a reaction, returns the reaction that started playing.
        StartPlayReactionEvent<override><native>:listenable(sidekick_reaction) = external {}

        # Signaled when the Sidekick ends playing a reaction, returns the reaction that played.
        StopPlayReactionEvent<override><native>:listenable(sidekick_reaction) = external {}

        # Get the agent that owns this Sidekick.
        GetOwningAgent<native><public>()<transacts><decides>:agent

        # Is the Sidekick visible?
        var Show<override>:logic = external {}

        # The Sidekick will run animations to react to the state of the player. Is this system enabled?
        var AutomaticReactionsEnabled<public>:logic = external {}

        # Sidekicks have a built-in player interaction; this can be disabled by setting this to false.
        var DefaultInteractionEnabled<public>:logic = external {}

    @available {MinUploadedAtFNVersion := 3800}

    # Spark mode will transform the entity into a floating spark.
    # The entity will enter `spark mode` whenever it enters impassable terrain or to reduce visual clutter.

        var SparkModeAlwaysActive<public>:logic = external {}

        BeginSparkModeEvent<native><public>:listenable(tuple()) = external {}

        # Signaled when the Sidekick exits spark mode
        EndSparkModeEvent<native><public>:listenable(tuple()) = external {}

        var ProgressTarget<public>:float = external {}

        var CurrentProgress<public>:float = external {}

        # This value maps to the 'ProgressRate' user option.

        var ProgressRate<public>:float = external {}

        # This value maps to the 'RegressRate' user option.

        #  Utilizing this value is not required, as 'CurrentProgress' can also be modified directly.
        var RegressRate<public>:float = external {}

        # This event is fired whenever 'CurrentProgress' reaches the 'ProgressTarget'.
        FillEvent<public>:listenable(tuple()) = external {}

        # This event is fired whenever 'CurrentProgress' reaches 0.
        EmptyEvent<public>:listenable(tuple()) = external {}

        ProgressChangeEvent<public>:listenable(float) = external {}

    # Used to generate random numbers between a minimum and maximum value. Events are signaled when numbers are generated.
    #  * *Value Limit 1* is the minimum value for generation.
    #  * *Value Limit 2* is the maximum value for generation.
    rng_device<public> := class<concrete><final>(creative_device_base):
        # Signaled when the generated number >= *Winning Value*.
        WinEvent<public>:listenable(tuple()) = external {}

        # Signaled when the generated number < *Winning Value*.
        LoseEvent<public>:listenable(tuple()) = external {}

        # Signaled when the generated number = maximum.
        RolledMaxEvent<public>:listenable(tuple()) = external {}

        # Signaled when the generated number = minimum.
        RolledMinEvent<public>:listenable(tuple()) = external {}

        # Enables this device.
        Enable<public>():void = external {}

        # Disables this device.
        Disable<public>():void = external {}

        # Randomly generate a number between *Value Limit 1* and *Value Limit 2*.
        #  * If the number is >= *Winning Value* then `WinEvent` is fired.
        #  * If the number is < *Winning Value* then `LoseEvent` is fired.
        #  * If the number = minimum then `RolledMinEvent` is fired.
        #  * If the number = maximum then `RolledMaxEvent` is fired.
        #  * `Agent` is used as the Instigator of the roll event.
        Activate<public>(Agent:agent):void = external {}

        # Randomly roll a number within the configured min + max value range.
        #  * If the number is >= *Winning Value* then `WinEvent` is fired.
        #  * If the number is < *Winning Value* then `LoseEvent` is fired.
        #  * If the number = minimum then `RolledMinEvent` is fired.
        #  * If the number = maximum then `RolledMaxEvent` is fired.
        Activate<public>():void = external {}

        # Cancels the active number generation.
        Cancel<public>():void = external {}

    # A device that generates a scoreboard stat that can be used by the game to determine Game End and Round End conditions.

# Appendix G — Global Utility Contract

## Global Utility.verse Contract (Project Infrastructure)

`Utility.verse` is not an engine feature. It is project-global infrastructure supplied by the user and must be treated as a canonical shared library.

When the actual `Utility.verse` file is available, inspect it in full before adding helper functionality. The following current public surface is provided as a compact reference from the supplied Utility file:

```verse
ToMultiplierString<public>(Value : float, DecimalPlaces : int) : string
FormatFloat<public>(Value : float, decimalplace : float) : float
StringToMessage<localizes><public>(String : string) : message
AgentNameMessage<localizes><public>(Agent : agent) : message
FormatTime<public>(TimeInSeconds : float) : string
FormatNumber<public>(Value : int, Shorthand : logic) : string
FormatNumberWithCommas<public>(Value : int) : string
FormatNumberShorthand<public>(Value : int) : string
FormatFloatTwoDecimals<public>(Value : float) : string
event_subscription := class
AwaitForEvent(Event : event(t), Callback : type {_(:t):void}, Subscription : event_subscription where t : type)<suspends> : void
(Event : event(t) where t : type).Subscribe<public>(Callback : type {_(:t):void}) : event_subscription
```

Canonical usage expectations:

- currency / large-number display → `FormatNumber`
- comma-formatted integer → `FormatNumberWithCommas`
- shorthand large-number display → `FormatNumberShorthand`
- multiplier display → `ToMultiplierString`
- floating-point display → `FormatFloat` / `FormatFloatTwoDecimals` where appropriate
- dynamic message creation → `StringToMessage`
- player-name message → `AgentNameMessage`
- timer/countdown text → `FormatTime`
- repeatable custom event subscriptions/cancellation → inspect the Utility subscription helpers before creating another abstraction

Do not create project-local equivalents of these helpers unless the actual Utility implementation has a documented limitation that requires a distinct behavior.

# Final AI Checklist

Before writing UEFN / Verse code:

- [ ] Requirements are sufficiently defined.
- [ ] UEFN-only APIs/workflows are being used.
- [ ] Current project digest has been checked when supplied.
- [ ] Existing codebase was searched before creating new infrastructure.
- [ ] Existing functions/events/managers/helpers were considered for reuse.
- [ ] No duplicate mutable state was introduced.
- [ ] Derived/inverse state is not stored redundantly.
- [ ] No no-rollback operation is incorrectly placed inside a failure context.
- [ ] `Utility.verse` was inspected/reused where applicable.
- [ ] Event-driven logic is preferred over unnecessary polling.
- [ ] Background tasks have a valid lifecycle.
- [ ] UI layer and Scene Graph layer are not being conflated.
- [ ] Experimental/deprecated/version-sensitive APIs are explicitly recognized.
- [ ] Performance implications were checked.
- [ ] Obsolete/dead code exposed by the change was removed when safe.
- [ ] Final codebase audit completed.

This document is a reference, not permission to invent missing APIs. When the actual project disagrees with this document, the actual project-generated API/source wins.
